reason: The component framework that redraws a browser-side mirror of host state is replaced by HTML fragments rendered on the host and swapped by id; each job it did (incremental updates while streaming, submission feedback, kept view state, routing) is placed on the host, in the browser's own features or in a small own script.
Its job, mounting the application tree and taking over the boot DOM, has no counterpart when every page is a complete HTTP response rendered by the host and updated by fragment swaps.

The store engine holds client copies of state and view preferences in localStorage; application state now stays on the host and view state goes to the URL, host preferences, the DOM or a small per-tab script store.

It exists only because React detects change by JavaScript object identity, so client stores need a helper that produces a new immutable object per update; Go projections produce new values and the event feed says what changed.
It is the JavaScript hook that binds a store snapshot to a React component in one file of ui-renderer; with no React components and no client stores there is nothing to bind.
It joins CSS class names conditionally inside JavaScript component code; a host template writes the class attribute directly with its own conditionals, so no library is involved.

Upstream virtualises the turn rail, the Trajectory table and the session inspector table, not the chat transcript; the Go host bounds every long list by paging on sequence number, windows around a target turn and bodies fetched on first open.

Kept by the owner's decision: the editor core gives the composer atomic reference chips inside plain text. The same library is vendored as its published, unpatched ES module files, embedded in the binary and loaded by one composer island through an import map; menu candidates, reference resolution, drafts and attachments move to the host.

Kept: plain-text editing behaviour (typing, deletion, line breaks, clipboard) is this package's, registered on the island's editor as upstream does; it is vendored unmodified and loaded by the composer island.

Kept: undo and redo with a paste as its own step and a picked reference as one step come from this package, registered on the island's editor; it is vendored unmodified, and its behaviour is shown in a real browser because the Go toolchain has no JavaScript test runner.

Kept: its one use, recognising a reference typed as plain text and styling it without making a chip, stays in the island; the host parses the same token rules at submit so a typed token and a chip resolve to the same target.

Kept: its one imported function combines the unregister functions of editor listeners, which the island calls when its element is removed; it is also imported by the other vendored packages, so it ships with them unmodified.
It exists only so one upstream unit test can run the JavaScript editor under Node without a DOM; the Go design tests host handlers in Go and tests any browser editing behaviour in a real browser.

The 648 KB patch carries a two-line fix for the caret hiding behind an on-screen keyboard, inflated because it rewrites two minified one-line builds. In the Go design vendored browser files must be byte-identical to a published release and may not be patched, so the patch does not exist; the behaviour it protected stays a requirement, met by a release that contains the fix or by the island's own code outside the vendored files, and shown on a touch device by a real-browser scenario.
Parsing Markdown text into a tree, in the client and in root documentation scripts, is done on the host by goldmark's parser; the tree never leaves the host.
Tables, task lists, strike-through, bare links and footnotes come from goldmark's shipped extensions, with an own strike-through rule that requires two tildes.
The GFM syntax half of the same feature set is goldmark's GFM extensions on the host; the bare-URL rule is one configured pattern, not a patched tokenizer.
Upstream imports the core emphasis construct to build its CJK-friendly bold rule; the Go renderer implements that rule as an own goldmark delimiter extension.
Character classification for the CJK bold rule and the math delimiters is done with Go's unicode package inside the own goldmark extensions.
Deciding whether a character is whitespace or punctuation for emphasis flanking is done with Go's unicode package in the own CJK delimiter extension.
Its one use, decoding a link destination so that a Windows path keeps its backslashes, becomes part of the own link renderer that recognises local-path destinations.
Normalising a link or image address before the scheme check is done with Go's net/url in the own link and image renderers, which apply an allow-list of schemes and fail closed on a parse error.
Its one use is whitespace handling inside upstream's tokenizer for backslash math delimiters; the passthrough extension takes those delimiters as configuration, so no tokenizer is written.
It is a table of numeric character codes and token names that JavaScript micromark extensions are written against; Go extension code uses rune literals and goldmark's own node kinds.
It contains only TypeScript type declarations for writing micromark extensions and has no runtime content; Go types come from the goldmark module.
Recognising dollar-delimited math in settled messages is done by the goldmark passthrough extension, configured with the dollar and backslash delimiter pairs and left out of the streaming grammar.
Turning math tokens into tree nodes is the same passthrough extension's job in goldmark, which yields nodes holding the raw TeX for the typesetting adapter.

Formulas are typeset on the host to MathML through one adapter whose first, provisional implementation is the treeblood module with a mandatory output filter; a KaTeX island is the named fallback if the coverage gate fails.
Code is tokenised on the host by chroma and written as class-named spans that the theme style sheet colours, so light and dark need no re-rendering and no highlighter runs in the browser.
The per-language grammar files, loaded on demand in the browser and patched in memory for Go and Perl, are replaced by chroma's embedded lexers, each rule of which has a match time limit.

Parsing terminal colour sequences in command output is own host code that also replays carriage return, backspace and erase-in-line and strips every other control sequence, because the candidate module also emits links and images from escape sequences.

Upstream sanitises only the HTML file preview in the browser; the Go host filters that document with an allow-list policy and serves it sandboxed with a policy header, and uses the same module as a last-step gate on every fragment built from untrusted text.

The patch makes a bare URL end before non-ASCII punctuation in the tokenizer. goldmark takes the bare-URL pattern as an option, so the rule is one configured regular expression with a test and no third-party file is edited.

The patch repeats the same bare-URL rule in a second package that finds URLs again after parsing. goldmark recognises a bare URL in one place, so one configured pattern covers it and the two copies cannot disagree.

Upstream uses 34 brand marks from the collection to label links to well-known hosts; the Go host keeps the fixed host table as a Go value and embeds the copied marks as one SVG sprite, with no module and no network fetch.
